THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECISION SAID WOULD DECIDE IT HAS BEEN TAKEN, AND IT OVERTURNS THE READING THAT NODE WAS LEANING TOWARD. `dec:idea-does-reflow2-need-a-byte-store-at-all-or-only-durability` closes: '🛑 WHAT IS UNMEASURED AND DECIDES IT: hydrate time. Parsing 8.4 MB of JSON, building the adjacency index and building the tantivy index, to first query. NOBODY HAS TAKEN IT.' Taken 2026-09-04, both arms in one process invocation, one machine, one minute, release build, on the 3,671-node / 18,069-edge committed export (11.5 MB):

    OPEN THE EXISTING ROCKSDB STORE   → first search:     168 ms
      open store 163.6 | point read 1.2 | search_design 4.1 | count(3694) 122.4

    HYDRATE FROM THE DOCUMENT ALONE   → first search:   2,672 ms
      parse 457.5 | import 2,208.2 | point read 0.1 | search_design 2.0

⭐ THE STORE IS ~16x FASTER TO FIRST QUERY, AND THAT IS A THIRD THING IT BUYS. That decision's own list of what a store buys is: (1) durability without a whole-document rewrite, (2) crash consistency, (3) larger-than-RAM, dismissed as irrelevant at this size. Its stated conclusion — 'for one person on one laptop, an embedded store buys DURABILITY AND CRASH-SAFETY AND NOTHING ELSE' — is now measurably incomplete. It also buys STARTUP: ~2.5 seconds saved on every session open, paid by every session of every project, not once.

⭐ AND THE COST IS WHERE THE EARLIER READING SAID IT WAS NOT. `fact:hydrate-cost-is-superlinear-in-edges-and-the-byte-store-is-not-the-bottleneck` is CONFIRMED and its title is still right: the byte store is not the bottleneck. IMPORT IS — 2,208 of 2,672 ms, 83% of it. Parsing 11.5 MB of JSON is 457 ms, 17%. So the document road is slow not because JSON is slow or storage is slow, but because rebuilding the adjacency index from scratch is.

THE FULL-TEXT INDEX IS THE CHEAP PART, which closes the bound that fact stated about itself. It warned every earlier figure was 'a LOWER BOUND for a hydrate that must answer search_design'. Measured, the bound is small: median of three runs each, no index 2,365 ms vs index 2,828 ms — the tantivy build costs ~460 ms, ~20%, and `search_design` itself answers in 2.0-4.1 ms either way.

⚠️ VARIANCE IS HIGH AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT WAS WRONG BECAUSE OF IT. Three no-index runs spanned 1,955-2,690 ms, a 37% spread on an idle-looking machine. The FIRST attempt at this measurement ran while the workspace test suite was still going (load 3-7 on 4 cores) and produced the impossible result that the INDEXED hydrate was FASTER than the unindexed one (2,409 vs 3,665 ms). Quote the medians, not a single run, and check `uptime` before believing either.

📌 SANITY CHECK WORTH KEEPING: the store reported 3,694 nodes against the document's 3,671. The difference is this session's uncommitted graph writes — the store is live and the export is a commit behind, exactly as it should be.

NOT ESTABLISHED, and it bounds what this decides: the store arm opens an index ALREADY BUILT ON DISK and the document arm builds one from nothing, which is the real asymmetry and is the point — but it means this measures SESSION START, not steady-state work. It says nothing about write throughput, nothing about what a crash costs, and nothing about whether 2.7 s would be acceptable if the trade bought something else. It also does not compare redb: no alternative engine was built or timed.
